‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ movie review: Familiar spin-off settles safely into dystopian comforts
 With moments of beauty and terror spread evenly in the second half, ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ doesn’t fully capitalise on the immense political reach of its dystopian-fuelled world
 Updated - November 20, 2026 05:07 pm IST 
 Shreyas Pande READ LATER 
 SEE ALL 
 Remove 
 Joseph Zada in a still from ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’
 | Photo Credit: Lionsgate Movies
 It is another day for another reaping in District 12. Marking the 50th Hunger Games, this time four tributes are chosen to participate in the fatal competition instead of two. Set 24 years before the first Hunger Games , which released in 2012, Sunrise on the Reaping opens with a risk of appearing too familiar. Even as its world belongs to the past, the events have a sense of regularity to them, seen so many times over the course of the five installments that have come before. It begins with that lethargic feeling of a franchise that refuses to let go, believing, rather plainly, that it still has many sunrises to see while its spark has lost long beyond the horizon.
 The beats are all too well-established, and it doesn’t help that screenwriter Billy Ray and director Michael Lesslie give in to that routine without any reinvention in the first half. It evokes memory of the grittier, handheld expository scenes from the 2012 film where J ennifer Lawrence ’s Katniss Everdeen volunteered herself for the competition. Here, 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) is caught in the mix without intending to. This is an outcome he would never have wished, least of all on his birthday, which coincides with the day of reaping.
 ‘The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes’ movie review: Middling addition to the franchise Haymitch parts with his lover, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), after we see them briefly sharing intimate moments in the dreamy wilderness. The pain of separation is not starkly registered even though Lesslie frames Haymitch looking towards Lenore from the train’s rain-drenched window. It is a rather forceful moment, considering how little emotional stake is established in their relationship. There is also a surprising streak of maturity to their love and it feels inorganic for their age. That’s why, even as their love story aims to become the essence of the film, the pay-off is never fruitful.
 The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (English)
 Director : Francis Lawrence Duration : 158 minutes Cast : Joseph Zada, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke Synopsis : 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy is chosen as one of the four tributes for the 50th Hunger Games as he brews a conspiracy to take on the tyranny of President Snow and destroy the arena. The narrative finds some strength once the games begin in the second half with Haymitch planning to sabotage and destroy the machinery that fuels it. He joins the plan during the training with Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), who is serving punishment for his past rebellions. Together with the cunning television director Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), they plan on resisting against the capitol and stopping the games once and for all.
 Jesse Plemons in a still from ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’
 | Photo Credit: 
 Lionsgate Movies
 The ambiguity of Plutarch’s words and actions is up for interpretation as the manipulative television director becomes a gateway of establishing control over the entire narrative. Even during reaping, it is at his insistence that tribute escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close) decides not to kill Haymitch, just because his girlfriend crying for him would make for a better story. When Haymitch thanks Plutarch for saving his life, the latter responds with surprise, “I was just doing my job.” Was he really?
 This is why it feels strangely dubious when he later reasons with Haymitch to trust him much later and urges him to go ahead with his plan. It feels even more so when he uses the punchline, “The smallest of successes can keep the fire of resistance alive,” to later convince President Snow (Ralph Fiennes) to make an important decision. This further reflects his manipulative tendencies and underlines the many conflicts of existing in a post-truth world, where anything can be manufactured with the right amount of narrative push.
 Ruth Madeley, Mark Ruffalo and Siân Heder on the fight behind Apple TV’s ‘Being Heumann’ Plemons also plays Plutarch without fully submitting to either of his shades. It is hard to tell when he truly means what he is saying, which adds a layered adaptability to his performance and makes him almost a symbol of the luring middlemen who control the narrative with their mighty nonchalance. Plutarch is also a character who could do more to underline the themes of authoritarianism that the franchise is known for exploring. But, as has been the case since its first part, even Sunrise on the Reaping doesn’t fully capitalise on the immense political reach of its dystopia-fuelled world.
 The film merely remains satisfied with toying around the plot without caring much about the deeper consequences. That ability to react more to the moment than the whole is seen even in the dramatic performance of Joseph. He brings in a feverish electricity to Haymitch, which works well in underlining his youthful anxieties but falls short of capturing the sweeping tragedy at his core, which turns him into the stern alcoholic played by Woody Harrelson in The Hunger Games (2012). Even then, Joseph’s finesse keeps Sunrise on the Reaping afloat throughout the long, thrilling third act. In between, smaller flashes of relief comes in seeing Kieran Culkin doing his tricks as a younger Caesar Flickerman while Ralph Fiennes maintains his sinister demeanor without moving his muscles a lot.
 Ralph Fiennes in a still from ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’
 | Photo Credit: 
 Lionsgate Movies
 The film has moments of beauty and terror spread evenly in the second half after it practically tick-marks its way from the first one. There is something to root for towards the end, even as Haymitch remains emotionally distant. The protagonist of a dystopian tale should feel closer, more palpable and life-like. Here, he comes across as one of the many instead of making his mark as the one and only. And Sunrise on the Reaping is not too different in that regard either.
 The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is currently running in theatres
